big: Shalini's EMI never changed in five years. Yet her bank's statement showed she now had two more years of payments left. The rate had risen, and the tenure quietly grew.

lines: My loan is floating. What happens when the Reserve Bank changes the repo rate?
Your rate follows at the next reset. Then either the EMI rises or the tenure stretches. Often the lender picks tenure, because you do not feel it.

intro: Same ₹30 lakh loan, five years in.
note: An unchanged EMI hid about two years and four months of extra payments.

title: Fixed and floating
stops: A floating rate follows a benchmark such as the repo rate
A rate rise can add years instead of raising the EMI
You must accept whatever the lender decides
Floating always costs less than fixed
caps: The rate is the benchmark plus the lender's spread, and it resets.
If the EMI stays put, the tenure grows, and you may not notice.
You can ask for a higher EMI, a longer tenure or a mix, or prepay a part.
Neither is always cheaper. Rates can fall or rise over a long loan.

q: The repo rate rises and Meena's floating-rate loan resets. What can happen?
opts: Her rate stays the same until the loan ends
Her loan is cancelled and the bank refunds her
Her rate rises, so the EMI or the tenure goes up
Her principal is cut by the same amount
why: A floating rate does not stay still, since it follows the benchmark at resets.
A rate change does not cancel a loan or bring any refund to the borrower.
The rate follows the benchmark, so either the EMI or the tenure has to give.
The principal is what she borrowed, and a rate change does not reduce it.

q: Rohan's EMI stayed the same after a rate rise. What is the likely reason?
opts: The tenure was lengthened without much notice
The rate did not change at all during those years
The bank paid the extra interest from its own funds
His principal was cleared by the bank after the reset
why: A longer tenure absorbs the higher interest, so the EMI can stay unchanged.
The rate rose, so something else had to take the higher cost.
Banks do not pay a borrower's extra interest from their own pocket.
The principal is not cleared by a rate change, so this does not fit.

q: Meena can afford a higher EMI after a rate rise. What is usually the cheaper choice?
opts: Let the tenure grow and keep the EMI
Stop paying until the rate falls again
Take a fresh loan to pay the old one
Raise the EMI, keep the tenure
why: A longer tenure feels painless but adds interest in every extra year.
Stopping payment brings penalties and harms her credit record.
A fresh loan adds new costs and fees, and does not fix the rate issue.
A higher EMI keeps the years short, so less interest builds up in the end.

q: Which borrower is better placed to choose a fixed rate?
opts: Someone who hopes to guess where rates are going
Someone whose budget cannot take a higher EMI
Someone who never reads the loan statement
Someone who wants the longest possible tenure
why: Guessing future rates is not a plan, and nobody can do it well.
A fixed rate gives a steady EMI, which suits a tight budget.
Reading the statement matters under both types of rate.
Tenure is a separate choice and does not decide fixed or floating.

pts: A floating rate is a benchmark plus a spread, and it resets.
An unchanged EMI can hide years of extra payments.
Read your loan statement once a year, and choose EMI or tenure on purpose.
